paragraphs.heading: The force between charges
paragraphs.text: Coulomb's law tells you how strong the force is between two electrically charged particles that are not moving. That force is usually called the electrostatic force, or the Coulomb force. The law was known before him, but the French physicist Charles-Augustin de Coulomb was the first to publish it, in 1785.

paragraphs.heading: How the rule works
paragraphs.text: The force grows with the product of the two charges, q₁ and q₂, and shrinks with the square of the distance r between them. A constant of proportionality, which may be called the Coulomb constant, sets the scale and depends on the unit of charge you use. The force points along the straight line joining the two charges. Charges of the same sign push apart, and charges of opposite sign pull together.

paragraphs.heading: A cousin of gravity
paragraphs.text: Because it is an inverse-square law, it looks like Newton's law of universal gravitation. But gravity only ever attracts, while electric forces can attract or repel, and gravity is much weaker. The law has been tested many times and holds over distances from 10⁻¹⁶ m to 10⁸ m.

paragraphs.heading: Amber and a new word
paragraphs.text: People around the ancient Mediterranean knew that amber rubbed with cat's fur would pick up feathers and scraps of paper. Around 600 BC, Thales of Miletus left the earliest written account of static electricity. In 1600 William Gilbert studied electricity and magnetism closely. He coined the word electricus, meaning like amber, for the pull an object shows after rubbing. From it came the English words electric and electricity, first printed in 1646.

paragraphs.heading: Guesses before Coulomb
paragraphs.text: Others suspected an inverse-square rule earlier. Joseph Priestley, after experiments with charged spheres, guessed in 1767 that the force varied with the inverse square of the distance. In 1769 John Robison reported that the push between two like-charged spheres varied as x⁻².06. Henry Cavendish found how the force depends on both distance and charge in the early 1770s, but did not publish it.

paragraphs.heading: The twisting balance
paragraphs.text: Coulomb measured the force with a torsion balance: a bar hung from its middle by a thin fiber that acts as a very weak twisting spring. His was an insulating rod with a metal-coated ball on one end, hung by a silk thread. He gave the ball a known charge and brought a second ball with the same kind of charge near it. The balls pushed apart and twisted the fiber, and he read the angle off a scale. Knowing how much force each amount of twist took, he worked out the force between the balls and arrived at his inverse-square law.

paragraphs.heading: Many charges at once
paragraphs.text: Coulomb then showed that the same law covers the pull between opposite charges. The law of superposition extends it to any number of point charges. The total force on one charge is just the vector sum of the forces each of the other charges would exert on it alone.
